summary: Frostline is a trend detective for Canada’s North. Every winter, northern communities rely on ice roads that exist only while the cold holds, but claims that “winters are changing” are rarely checked properly. Frostline lets anyone pick a place on a map, pull decades of NASA temperature data, and see what changed, by how much, and how sure we can be. It does this with trend rates, confidence intervals and significance tests, then exports a report anyone can verify. Using 46 years of NASA MERRA-2 data through Giovanni, we found autumn near Yellowknife warming about 0.6 °C per decade, the only one of seven seasons that held up after correction. Government records also show the Dettah ice road opening about 9 days later per decade. Frostline turns NASA Earth data into honest, checkable evidence for students, northern communities and anyone curious.
details:
Every winter, communities across Canada’s North build roads out of ice, across frozen lakes and rivers. These roads carry food, fuel and supplies, and they only exist while the cold holds. People often say northern winters are changing, but checking that claim honestly is hard. It means finding the right NASA data, cleaning daily records, fitting trends, testing significance, and knowing what the numbers cannot say. Frostline makes that whole investigation possible in a few clicks.

What it does and how it works
Frostline is a trend detective for the North. A user picks any place between 50° and 75°N on an interactive map, and Frostline pulls decades of NASA temperature data for that exact grid cell. It then measures the rate of change per decade, shows a 95% confidence interval, and runs a Mann-Kendall significance test: exactly what the challenge asks for. Every result gets a plain-language verdict (“supported” or “not resolved”) and exports as an Evidence Brief that anyone can download, check and reproduce.

For our worked case study near Yellowknife, we used 46 years of NASA MERRA-2 data extracted through NASA Giovanni. Autumn warmed about +0.60 °C per decade (95% interval 0.23 to 0.97). It was the only one of seven seasons tested that held up after correcting for multiple tests. Alongside it, 32 winters of Government of the Northwest Territories records show the Dettah ice road opening about 9 days later per decade.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Students and the public learn to test a climate claim properly, with real NASA data.
  • Northern communities and planners get clear, checkable facts about winter-road seasons.
  • Anyone curious can investigate any place in the North in minutes, not weeks.

Our goal is to replace “winters feel shorter” with “here is what changed, by how much, and how sure we are.”

How it is creative
Most trend tools hand you a slope. Frostline is built to be trusted: it corrects for running many tests so lucky flukes don’t count, checks NASA data against a real ground station (correlation 0.92), and places climate and road records side by side so users can judge the evidence themselves. Every number on screen can be rebuilt from raw data, byte for byte.

Tools and technologies
Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Plotly, Folium and pydeck. NASA data comes from NASA Giovanni (MERRA-2 M2TMNXSLV) and the NASA POWER API. Ground and road data come from Environment and Climate Change Canada (Yellowknife A station) and the NWT Bureau of Statistics. The statistics are Theil-Sen trends, Mann-Kendall tests, block-bootstrap confidence intervals and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. The project includes 209 automated tests, and AI tools (Claude) assisted with development.

What our team considered
We focused on scientific honesty and accessibility. We designed Frostline for non-experts, explained every number in plain language, and checked NASA data against ground truth. We also deliberately kept it as an evidence tool: it does not predict ice conditions or road safety. Next, we plan to expand to all 17 NWT winter roads, add NASA MODIS snow cover, and seek independent expert review.
